html:
I’ve been reading the Steve Jobs biography lately, and Jobs and Woz strike me as textbook examples of the two types the question describes. Let me say a few words about them.

Woz was a brilliant engineer, and both his parents were highly educated. You could say the core technology of the Apple I and Apple II was his work alone. Outside of technology, the young Woz was extremely shy, a total nerd.

Jobs understood technology too, but nowhere near as well as Woz. What he was brilliant at was negotiating and persuading people (even when he didn’t understand the subject or was simply wrong). He was supremely self-confident, quite arrogant, and, more importantly, he had insight. That insight is why, decades later, Apple is still a god-like presence in several markets, from computers, phones and tablets to wireless earbuds, and why it turned the music industry upside down.

You have to admit that a duo like Woz and Jobs may be the ideal combination for a startup: one rock-solid on the technology inside, the other a force of nature on the outside.

Jobs’s technical skills could never have won people over. Woz mentioned more than once that Jobs didn’t understand technology, and the core members of the original Macintosh team were all people like Woz, technically far ahead of Jobs.

And yet everyone meekly did what Jobs told them. For the core team, every Apple product launch was an ordeal to be survived. On top of the normal feature requirements came all of Jobs’s strange demands: produce a decent demo the night before the launch event; he doesn’t like the color of a certain font; the icons aren’t rounded enough…

Yet he had this magic that let him boss around all kinds of tech heavyweights.

First, the people he hired thought the way he did: people a little obsessive about technology, with a vision of and passion for truly awesome products. When he was building the Macintosh, for example, he would take candidates into the office and pull the cloth off the Macintosh, and if their eyes didn’t light up in that instant, they basically didn’t get an offer. That’s why he could push these people to the limit. Working “996” (9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week) was routine, and on top of that he regularly told them they were garbage and that what they’d made was bullshit.

Second, his personal charisma. In social situations we all tend to listen to people who are confident, who state their views clearly and argue well. A great many people hated Jobs, but those who worshipped him would follow him through anything.

Finally, and I think most importantly, there was his insight into the industry (vision!) and his unwavering conviction. Computers go without saying; they were the product Apple was built on. Later came the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Every time word got out that Jobs was moving into a new industry, it seemed Bill Gates and lots of other people and media outlets would stand up and say Jobs was crazy, that he couldn’t pull it off, that the product was pointless. And then they were proven spectacularly wrong. His conviction let him stick to his ideas when everyone was against him, overcome difficulties inside and outside the company, cursing, pounding the table and going to court along the way, and then make the most awesome products.

So if you had to classify Jobs, he was a manager whose technical skills weren’t up to much. But the people under him who doubted his technical ability discovered, time and again, that although their boss wasn’t a particularly nice person and working for him was painful, he was right most of the time, and the things they made with him turned out to be astonishingly good. Naturally, they fell into line and worked their hearts out.


I highly recommend the Steve Jobs biography. The man was a once-in-a-generation genius and an out-and-out weirdo. I’m nearly done with it, and I’m about to become an Apple fanboy…
